title: Paediatric basic life support
blurb: How CPR changes for infants and children: five rescue breaths first, then 15:2, compressing one third of the chest depth.
question: A 6-year-old collapses in the waiting room after an appointment. She is unresponsive and not breathing normally. You and the dentist are trained in paediatric life support. How does your CPR differ from what you would do for her father?

teach.body: In adults, cardiac arrest usually starts with a heart problem. In children it usually comes at the end of a breathing problem: the child runs out of oxygen and then the heart stops. That's why paediatric BLS starts by putting oxygen back in, with five rescue breaths, before compressions begin, and why breaths stay a bigger share of CPR (15:2 instead of 30:2). The technique also changes with the size of the child.

items.label: Child technique
items.sub: Head tilt, chin lift; one or two hands

items.label: Paediatric AED mode or pads
items.sub: Adult AED if none, for children over 1

items.label: Adult technique
items.sub: 5–6 cm deep, never more than 6 cm

steps.label: Safe? Responsive?
steps.sub: Speak and gently stimulate; shout for help

steps.label: Call 999
steps.sub: Straight away, on speaker, or a colleague calls

steps.label: 5 rescue breaths
steps.sub: Watch for the chest to rise

steps.label: AED on
steps.sub: Second rescuer brings it; paediatric mode if available

teach.caption: RCUK 2025: call 999 as soon as the child is found unresponsive, then check breathing. With two rescuers, one starts CPR while the other calls and brings the AED. Rescuers not trained in paediatric BLS use 30:2 after the five breaths.

items.label: of the chest depth, at least

teach.caption: In the practice you'll give breaths with a pocket mask or a bag-valve-mask with a child-sized face mask, rather than mouth to mouth.

teach.h: Why the infant head stays neutral
teach.body: An infant's head is large compared with the body and their airway is soft and narrow. Tipping the head right back can kink the airway shut, so infants are kept in a neutral position (the face looking straight up). Older children need a gentle head tilt and chin lift, as in adults. For compressions, push on the lower half of the breastbone to at least one third of the chest's depth: two thumbs with your hands encircling the chest for an infant (RCUK 2025), the heel of one or both hands for a child.

teach.h: Using an AED on a child
teach.body: An AED can be used on children. For children under about 25 kg (roughly 8 years), use paediatric pads or the paediatric mode if your machine has one. RCUK's dental quality standards say that if no paediatric facility is available, a standard adult AED may be used on a child over 1 year old. Practices that treat children should consider having a paediatric facility.

teach.text: Don't give the adult sequence to a child by habit. The two differences examiners test most: FIVE initial rescue breaths before compressions, and 15:2 (not 30:2) for trained rescuers. Depth is described as one third of the chest, not a fixed number of centimetres.

items: Children usually arrest from lack of oxygen, so breaths come first.
Unresponsive: call 999 first, then open the airway and check breathing (no more than 10 s).
Not breathing normally: 5 rescue breaths before any compressions.
Then 15:2 if trained in PBLS (30:2 otherwise), at 100–120 a minute.
Compress at least one third of the chest depth; adolescents 5–6 cm.
Infant: neutral head, two encircling thumbs. Child: head tilt, one or two hands.
AED: paediatric mode under 25 kg; an adult AED may be used over 1 year if none.

summary: You can now explain why children arrest differently, follow the paediatric BLS sequence with five initial rescue breaths and 15:2 CPR, adapt the airway, breaths and compression technique for infants and children, compress to one third of the chest depth, and use an AED safely on a child.

A.q: A child collapses in the practice and is not breathing normally. You are trained in paediatric BLS. After opening the airway, what should you do first?
options: Feel for a pulse for a minute
A.why: Paediatric BLS starts with 5 initial rescue breaths, because child arrests usually follow a lack of oxygen.

whyNot.0: Starting with compressions is the adult sequence.
whyNot.2: Two breaths are given in each cycle of CPR, but the start is five rescue breaths.
whyNot.3: A long pulse check delays CPR; breathing decides whether to start.

A.q: What compression to ventilation ratio should a trained dental team use for a child in cardiac arrest?
A.why: Rescuers trained in paediatric BLS use 15 compressions to 2 breaths after the initial 5 rescue breaths.

whyNot.0: 30:2 is the adult ratio, or the fallback for rescuers not trained in paediatric BLS.
whyNot.1: 15:1 isn't an RCUK ratio; two breaths are given each cycle.
whyNot.2: 5:1 is an outdated ratio and is not used.

A.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an infant in cardiac arrest?
options: At least one third of the chest depth
Exactly 5–6 cm, the same as an adult
About one tenth of the chest depth
Just enough to see the skin move
A.why: For infants and children, compress to at least one third of the front-to-back depth of the chest.

whyNot.1: 5–6 cm is the adult and adolescent depth, and would be too deep for an infant.
whyNot.2: One tenth is far too shallow to move blood.
whyNot.3: Skin movement alone is too shallow to squeeze the heart.

B.q: Why does paediatric BLS begin with rescue breaths, unlike adult BLS?
options: Children's hearts are too small to compress
Child arrests usually follow lack of oxygen
Compressions are not used in young children
Breaths are safer for the rescuer to give
B.why: Most child arrests are caused by a breathing problem leading to lack of oxygen, so oxygen is restored first.

whyNot.0: Children's hearts can be compressed; compressions follow the breaths.
whyNot.2: Compressions are a core part of paediatric CPR.
whyNot.3: Rescuer safety isn't the reason; the cause of the arrest is.

B.q: You are giving rescue breaths to a 4-month-old baby. How should the head be positioned?
options: Tilted back as far as possible
B.why: An infant's airway is soft and easily kinked, so the head is kept neutral rather than tilted back.

whyNot.0: Over-tilting can kink an infant's soft airway closed.
whyNot.1: Turning the head to one side doesn't open the airway for breaths.
whyNot.3: Bending the chin to the chest closes the airway.

B.q: A member of staff who is trained only in adult BLS must give CPR to a child. What does RCUK advise?
options: Wait for a trained colleague first
B.why: Rescuers not trained in paediatric BLS should give the five rescue breaths then continue at 30:2; doing adult-style CPR is far better than nothing.

whyNot.0: Waiting means no oxygen or blood flow; CPR must start now.
whyNot.1: Breaths matter especially in children, whose arrests usually follow lack of oxygen.
whyNot.3: Breaths alone don't circulate blood; compressions are essential.

C.q: Which compression technique is appropriate for an infant under 1 year old?
options: Two thumbs, hands encircling the chest
Heel of both hands, fingers interlocked
One fist on the centre of the chest
Heel of one hand on the upper chest
C.why: RCUK 2025 recommends the two-thumb encircling technique for infants, on the lower half of the breastbone.

whyNot.1: Two interlocked hands is the adult technique and far too forceful for an infant.
whyNot.2: A fist isn't a recommended CPR technique for any age.
whyNot.3: The upper chest is the wrong place, and one hand is used for older children, not infants.

C.q: A 5-year-old (about 18 kg) is in cardiac arrest and the practice AED has a paediatric mode. What should you do?
options: Don't use the AED on a child this young
Use the AED with the paediatric mode on
Use adult mode, as children need more energy
Wait until the paramedics bring their own
C.why: For children under about 25 kg (roughly 8 years), use paediatric pads or the paediatric mode if available.

whyNot.0: AEDs can and should be used on children in cardiac arrest.
whyNot.2: Children need a lower energy dose; the paediatric mode provides it. Adult mode is only a fallback when no paediatric option exists.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays defibrillation; use the practice AED now.

C.q: A 15-year-old who has gone through puberty is in cardiac arrest. How deep should compressions be?
C.why: Adolescents are treated like adults for compression depth: 5–6 cm and never more than 6 cm.

whyNot.0: 1–2 cm is far too shallow to move blood.
whyNot.1: 2–3 cm is still too shallow for an adolescent.
whyNot.2: Compressions should never be deeper than 6 cm.

reteach.title: Refill the tank, then start the engine
reteach.question: A child's heart usually stops because the oxygen 'tank' ran dry. What would you do first if a car stalled because it ran out of fuel?

blocks.body: If a car stops because it ran out of petrol, cranking the engine won't help until you put fuel in. Children are similar: their hearts usually stop because they ran out of oxygen. So you fill the tank first with five rescue breaths, then start pumping. Because the tank empties quickly in a small body, breaths keep coming more often: 2 breaths after every 15 compressions instead of every 30.

blocks.h: Child vs adult at a glance

blocks.text: Size the technique to the child: two encircling thumbs for an infant, one or two hands for a child. The aim is always one third of the chest depth.

explain.body: Once 999 has been called, open the airway. If the child is not breathing normally, give five rescue breaths, watching the chest rise with each. This puts oxygen back in before compressions begin.

test.q: How many initial rescue breaths are given in paediatric BLS?
test.why: RCUK paediatric BLS starts with five initial rescue breaths.

whyNot.0: Two breaths are given in each CPR cycle, not as the initial breaths.
whyNot.1: Three isn't part of the RCUK sequence.
whyNot.3: Ten would delay compressions; the guideline is five.

explain.body: After the five breaths, trained rescuers give 15 compressions then 2 breaths at 100–120 compressions a minute. Anyone not trained in paediatric BLS uses 30:2 instead.

test.q: Which statement about CPR ratios for children is correct?
test.why: Rescuers trained in paediatric BLS use 15:2; others use 30:2 after the five initial breaths.

whyNot.1: Untrained rescuers may use 30:2, which is better than nothing.
whyNot.2: 30:2 is the fallback, not the standard for trained teams.
whyNot.3: Ratios do apply; 15:2 is the trained ratio.

explain.body: Infant: neutral head, breaths over mouth and nose, two encircling thumbs. Child: head tilt and chin lift, one or two hands. Both: at least one third of the chest depth, on the lower half of the breastbone.

test.q: For rescue breaths on an infant without a mask, where does the rescuer's mouth go?
test.why: An infant's face is small, so the rescuer seals over both the mouth and nose.

whyNot.0: Mouth only, pinching the nose, is the technique for older children.
whyNot.1: Nose only isn't the infant technique.
whyNot.3: This wouldn't deliver air to the airway at all.

explain.body: Use paediatric pads or mode for children under about 25 kg (roughly 8 years). If there is no paediatric facility, a standard adult AED may be used on a child over 1 year.

test.q: The practice AED has no paediatric pads or mode. A 3-year-old is in cardiac arrest. What should you do?
options: Don't use the AED on a child
Cut the adult pads in half
test.why: RCUK's dental quality standards say a standard adult AED may be used on a child over 1 year if no paediatric facility is available.

whyNot.1: Defibrillation can save a child's life; don't withhold it.
whyNot.2: Pads must never be cut; it damages them.
whyNot.3: Delaying defibrillation reduces the chance of survival.
